longQuestions: A function is a named block of statements that performs a specific task; it can take arguments and return a value, and can be called many times.
Built-in (library) functions are already defined in C++ header files and are used directly, e.g. sqrt(), pow() in <cmath>, strlen() in <cstring>, getch() in <conio.h>.

The function prototype (declaration) tells the compiler the function's name, return type and parameter types before it is used; it ends with a semicolon and may omit parameter names: int sum(int, int);
The function declarator is the first line of the function definition; it has no semicolon and is followed by the function body: int sum(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
So the only difference is the semicolon (and that the prototype need not name the parameters).

A default argument is a value given to a parameter in the function declaration; it is used automatically when the caller does not pass that argument, e.g. void line(char ch = '*', int n = 10); — line(); prints 10 stars, line('#', 5); prints 5 #.
Advantages: the same function can be called with fewer arguments; simplifies calls when values are usually the same; reduces the need to write overloaded functions; makes programs easier to extend.

Disadvantages: default arguments must be the rightmost parameters; can make the meaning of a call less clear; may cause ambiguity with overloaded functions; a wrong default may silently give wrong results.

Function overloading means defining two or more functions with the same name but different parameter lists (number, type or order of parameters). The compiler decides which one to call from the arguments.
Data types of arguments — functions can have the same name if their parameter types differ: void show(int x); void show(float x); show(5) calls the first, show(2.5f) the second.
Number of arguments — functions can be overloaded by a different number of parameters: int sum(int a, int b); int sum(int a, int b, int c);
Order of arguments — if the types appear in a different order the functions are different: void print(int a, char c); void print(char c, int a); The return type alone cannot be used to overload.
